subject: Guerrini et al. (2001)
object: Guerrini et al. (2001) described a pedigree with 8 affected individuals who had a non-progressive disorder beginning between ages 12 and 50 years. All patients had predominantly distal, semi-continuous rhythmic myoclonus and generalized tonic-clonic seizures, and 3 had complex partial seizures. Most rarely had seizures and had normal cognition, but 3 with intractable seizures had mild mental retardation. The authors named the disorder autosomal dominant cortical myoclonus and epilepsy (ADCME).

subject: Guerrini et al. (2001)
object: Guerrini et al. (2001) found that all affected members of the ADCME pedigree had frontotemporal as well as generalized interictal EEG abnormalities. Neurophysiologic studies suggested a cortical origin for the myoclonus: back-averaging showed EEG waves whose frequency matched the EMG bursts. In 5 patients, EMG and EEG over the contralateral rolandic area showed significant coherence at 8 to 25 Hz, with EEG activity preceding EMG activity by 8 to 15 ms. In 2 individuals, ipsilateral EEG–EMG coherence was consistent with transcallosal spread of myoclonic activity.

subject: Guerrini et al. (2001)
object: Guerrini et al. (2001) found an enhanced C-reflex at rest and high-amplitude somatosensory and visual evoked potentials in patients with ADCME. Compared with controls, patients had a significantly reduced resting motor threshold to transcranial magnetic stimulation (38%) and a significantly shorter post-motor evoked potential silent period (101 ms vs 137 ms in controls). The authors suggested that these findings reflect diffuse cortical hyperexcitability that particularly involves frontotemporal circuits.

subject: Guerrini et al. (2001)
object: Guerrini et al. (2001) found that ADCME was inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern with high penetrance in the family they studied.

subject: Guerrini et al. (2001)
object: In a genome-wide linkage analysis of the ADCME family, Guerrini et al. (2001) identified a 12.4-cM critical region on 2p11.1-q12.2 between markers D2S2161 and D2S1897. The maximum 2-point lod score was 3.46 at theta = 0.0 for marker D2S2175, and the multipoint lod score reached 3.74 around D2S2175.

subject: Guerrini et al. (2001)
object: Guerrini et al. (2001) excluded linkage of their family to the familial adult myoclonic epilepsy locus on chromosome 8q23.3-q24. Together with the new localization to 2cen and the different phenotype, the authors concluded that ADCME is a new epilepsy syndrome.

subject: de Falco et al. (2003)
object: de Falco et al. (2003) reported a clinical and electrophysiologic study of 2 Italian families with benign adult familial myoclonic epilepsy (BAFME). They found linkage to chromosome 2p11.1-q12.2.

subject: de Falco et al. (2003)
object: de Falco et al. (2003) noted that BAFME had been mapped to chromosome 8q24. Their finding of linkage to 2p11.1-q12.2 in 2 Italian families supported genetic heterogeneity and the existence of non-Japanese families with BAFME. They suggested that this locus might be allelic with the autosomal dominant cortical myoclonus and epilepsy (ADCME) syndrome.

subject: Striano et al. (2004)
object: Striano et al. (2004) described a new family with benign adult familial myoclonic epilepsy (BAFME) and reported suggestive linkage to chromosome 2p11.1-q12.2, with a lod score of 1.55.

subject: Striano et al. (2004)
object: Striano et al. (2004) concluded that their observation would confirm that BAFME is a worldwide, genetically heterogeneous condition, probably with Japanese families linked to 8q24 and European families to 2p11.1-q12.2.

subject: Striano et al. (2004)
object: Striano et al. (2004) described BAFME as an autosomal dominant condition characterized by cortical tremor and generalized seizures.

subject: Striano et al. (2005)
object: Striano et al. (2005) reported a 5-generation family from Naples, Italy, with cortical tremor, myoclonus, and epilepsy. Eleven members, aged 24 to 56 years (mean 39.2 years), had hand tremor and myoclonus, and 6 of them also had generalized seizures. Electrophysiologic study confirmed cortical reflex myoclonus in all affected members.

subject: Striano et al. (2005)
object: Striano et al. (2005) found giant somatosensory evoked potential components and an enhanced long loop reflex I in 3 presymptomatic members of the family. These members developed hand tremor and upper-limb myoclonus after 1.5 years of follow-up.

subject: Striano et al. (2005)
object: In the Italian family with cortical tremor, myoclonus, and epilepsy, Striano et al. (2005) found significant linkage to chromosome 2p, with a maximum lod score of 5.9.

subject: Saint-Martin et al. (2008)
object: Saint-Martin et al. (2008) refined the chromosome 2p11.1-q12.2 locus responsible for cortical tremor associated with epilepsy.

subject: Saint-Martin et al. (2008)
object: Saint-Martin et al. (2008) excluded candidate genes within the refined 2p11.1-q12.2 locus for cortical tremor associated with epilepsy.

subject: Madia et al. (2008)
object: Madia et al. (2008) genotyped 53 affected individuals from 5 BAFME families from southern Italy, one of them not previously reported. They used microsatellite markers spanning chromosomes 2p11.1-q12.2 and 8q23.1-q24.11. Multipoint linkage analysis found significant linkage to 2p11.1-q12.2, with a maximum cumulative lod score of 18.5 for markers D2S2161 and D2S388.

subject: Madia et al. (2008)
object: Madia et al. (2008) found that the haplotype '5332' of the adjacent markers D2S388, D2S2216, D2S113, and D2S2175 segregated with the disease in all 5 southern Italian BAFME families. They concluded that these families carry the same mutation inherited from a common ancestor.

subject: Madia et al. (2008)
object: In a preliminary genotype-phenotype analysis, Madia et al. (2008) found only minor clinical differences among patients carrying the founder disease haplotype. They suggested that other factors do not markedly influence the expressivity of the founder mutation.

subject: Madia et al. (2008)
object: Madia et al. (2008) described benign adult familial myoclonic epilepsy (BAFME) as an autosomal dominant condition characterized by shivering-like tremors of cortical origin, myoclonus, and epilepsy.

subject: Suppa et al. (2009)
object: Suppa et al. (2009) described an Italian family with familial cortical myoclonic tremor with epilepsy (FCMTE). Clinically affected family members had limb and voice tremor, seizures, and myoclonus of the eyelids during blinking. Neuropsychological testing showed visuospatial impairment, which the authors suggested might be due to temporal lobe dysfunction. Neurophysiologic findings suggested increased excitability of the primary motor cortex with normal sensorimotor integration.

subject: Suppa et al. (2009)
object: In the Italian FCMTE family, Suppa et al. (2009) excluded linkage to the 8q24 locus. Affected members shared a common haplotype spanning 14.5 Mb in the pericentromeric region of chromosome 2.

subject: Suppa et al. (2009)
object: Suppa et al. (2009) excluded the 8q24 locus by linkage analysis in an Italian FCMTE family. This is evidence of genetic heterogeneity, with the family instead sharing a haplotype on pericentromeric chromosome 2.

subject: Coppola et al. (2011)
object: Coppola et al. (2011) evaluated the clinical, electrophysiologic, and treatment data of 14 patients from 3 families with autosomal dominant cortical tremor, myoclonus, and epilepsy linked to chromosome 2p11.1-q12.2. Mean age at onset was 20.2 years (range 11 to 40 years), and mean follow-up was 14.0 years. Myoclonus worsened gradually in 10 patients (71.4%), and severity correlated with disease duration and patient age. Two patients older than 80 years had myoclonus that interfered with walking on their own. Six patients (42.8%) had seizures, usually between the second and sixth decades of life, and more than a third had psychiatric and neuropsychological dysfunction.

subject: Coppola et al. (2011)
object: Coppola et al. (2011) found that, over the long term, EEG background activity slowed progressively as the myoclonus worsened. In contrast, paroxysmal activity and photosensitivity were most evident in the intermediate phases of the disease. The authors concluded that the disorder shows slight age-dependent progression. They suggested that the name 'familial or autosomal dominant cortical tremor, myoclonus, and epilepsy' (FCTME/ADCME) was more appropriate.

subject: Crompton et al. (2012)
object: Crompton et al. (2012) described a 6-generation kindred of European descent with familial adult myoclonic epilepsy, ascertained in New Zealand and Australia. All 55 affected members had fine hand tremor, with onset typically in adolescence (median age 15 years; range 4-60 years). Proximal myoclonus was present in 44 of 55 (80%), arising later than the hand tremor (median 17 years; range 5-60 years), and generalized tonic-clonic seizures occurred in 8 of 55 (15%), with a median age at onset of 43.5 years (range 18-76 years). Neurophysiologic testing confirmed features of cortical reflex myoclonus.

subject: Crompton et al. (2012)
object: Crompton et al. (2012) concluded that the most common FAME phenotype in this large family was mild postural hand tremor resembling essential tremor combined with subtle proximal myoclonus. Generalized tonic-clonic seizures were uncommon and occurred around sleep onset following severe generalized myoclonus.

subject: Crompton et al. (2012)
object: In the large Australian/New Zealand FAME kindred, Crompton et al. (2012) narrowed the FAME2 locus on chromosome 2 to a 13.3-Mb interval containing 99 known protein-coding genes.

subject: Licchetta et al. (2013)
object: Licchetta et al. (2013) described a large family with familial cortical myoclonic tremor and epilepsy (FCMTE). Of the 127 family members, 25 were affected (9 males, 16 females), and 16 of the 19 living affected members were studied (mean age 47.8 years). Cortical myoclonic tremor was associated with generalized seizures in 10 patients (62.5%). Mean age at onset was 28.1 years for cortical myoclonic tremor and 33.8 years for seizures. Four patients (25%) reported slow progression of the tremor, with severe gait impairment in 1, and psychiatric disorders of variable severity occurred in 37.5% of cases.

subject: Licchetta et al. (2013)
object: Licchetta et al. (2013) performed polygraphic studies in 15 family members and back-averaging and somatosensory evoked potentials with C-reflex studies in 4. Rhythmic bursts at 7 to 15 Hz were recorded in all 11 affected members tested, and the additional studies showed a cortical origin of myoclonus in all patients tested. Generalized epileptiform discharges were recorded in 25% of cases and a photoparoxysmal response in 31%.

subject: Licchetta et al. (2013)
object: Licchetta et al. (2013) genotyped 30 family members with microsatellite markers at the FCMTE1 (8q), FCMTE2 (2p), and FCMTE3 (5p) loci. They established linkage to the FCMTE2 locus on chromosome 2p11.1-q12.2 and narrowed the critical interval to a 10.4-Mb segment. This reduced the number of positional candidate genes to 59.

subject: Licchetta et al. (2013)
object: Licchetta et al. (2013) found that the family carried a founder haplotype identical to the one previously seen in FCMTE2 families from the same geographic area. They concluded that this confirms a founder effect in Italian families.

subject: Henden et al. (2016)
object: Henden et al. (2016) performed identity-by-descent (IBD) analysis on high-density SNP array data from a FAME cohort of 10 European families and 1 Australian/New Zealander family, 8 of which had known disease loci. By finding IBD regions shared by several families, they narrowed the FAME2 locus to a 9.78-Mb interval within 2p11.2-q11.2. They also suggested candidate disease genes by prioritizing genes with gene co-expression analysis.

subject: Henden et al. (2016)
object: Henden et al. (2016) gave additional evidence of a founder effect in 4 Italian families with FAME2. They also found allelic heterogeneity at the FAME2 locus, with at least 4 distinct founders responsible for the disease.

subject: Henden et al. (2016)
object: Henden et al. (2016) described familial adult myoclonus epilepsy (FAME) as a rare autosomal dominant disorder. It is characterized by adult onset, involuntary muscle jerks, cortical myoclonus and occasional seizures. They noted that FAME is genetically heterogeneous, with more than 70 families reported worldwide and 5 potential disease loci.

subject: Corbett et al. (2019)
object: Corbett et al. (2019) described FAME as characterized by cortical myoclonic tremor and overt myoclonic and later generalized tonic-clonic seizures, with onset in the second to third decade, variable expressivity within and between families, and anticipation in some families. Seizures are typically controlled with antiepileptic drugs for generalized epilepsies, although drug resistance occurs rarely.

subject: Corbett et al. (2019)
object: Corbett et al. (2019) summarized clinical data on 22 FAME2 families (Australian/New Zealand, Italian, Iraqi and Israeli of Sephardic Jewish ancestry, South African, French/Spanish, French, and Syrian). Myoclonus/cortical tremor was present in nearly all affected individuals, whereas the frequency of tonic-clonic seizures varied from 15 to 100% between families; focal seizures occurred in a minority. In the large Australian/New Zealand family (family 1), 55 individuals were affected with mean onset 18.6 years (range 4-59), all had myoclonus/cortical tremor, 8/55 had tonic-clonic seizures, and 2/55 had focal seizures.

subject: Corbett et al. (2019)
object: In affected members of 3 FAME2 families (Australian/New Zealand, Italian, French/Spanish), Corbett et al. (2019) used whole-genome sequencing with repeat-expansion detection (ExpansionHunter and exSTRa) to identify an expansion of an ATTTT repeat with insertion of an ATTTC repeat in intron 1 of STARD7. The ATTTC repeat was absent from 69 control genomes. By repeat-primed PCR, the ATTTC expansion was found in 137/137 affected individuals from 16 previously reported FAME2 families and in 20/20 familial cases from 6 further families and 1 of 52 unrelated singletons, for a total of 158 affected individuals from 22 families; 2 of 24 unaffected relatives tested positive, both from younger generations and likely presymptomatic. The expansion was not amplified in 28 control DNA samples.

subject: STARD7 intronic ATTTC repeat insertion/expansion with ATTTT expansion, intron 1
Corbett et al. (2019)
object: Corbett et al. (2019) used long-read sequencing to characterize the repeat structure as (AAATG)n[N](AAAAT)n on the forward strand. In one patient from family 1, a PacBio read contained 274 AAATG and 387 AAAAT repeats and a nanopore read contained 345 AAATG and 390 AAAAT repeats, suggesting somatic variability; in a patient from family 5, a read showed 588 AAATG and 340 AAAAT repeats (4,645 bp). The endogenous ATTTT repeat was variable in length in the normal population.

subject: Corbett et al. (2019)
object: Corbett et al. (2019) found the STARD7 ATTTC repeat in 2 families carrying the previously proposed ADRA2B variant (c.675_686delTGGTGGGGCTTTinsGTTTGGCAG), strongly suggesting that the ADRA2B allele is not causative.

subject: Corbett et al. (2019)
object: Corbett et al. (2019) found evidence of anticipation in the large Australian/New Zealand FAME2 family: median onset was 30 years in generation III, 17 years in generation IV, and 12 years in generation V.

subject: Corbett et al. (2019)
object: Corbett et al. (2019) found no change in STARD7 mRNA (qPCR, RNA-seq) or protein levels (Western blot) in patient-derived fibroblasts, and no reads containing ATTTC repeats in RNA-seq data. They suggested that the repeat sequence alone is pathogenic, independent of an effect on the encompassing gene, possibly via RNA toxicity as proposed for other ATTTC expansion disorders.

subject: Corbett et al. (2019)
object: Corbett et al. (2019) reported that the ATTTC repeat-primed PCR assay was diagnostic for FAME with 100% sensitivity in all families with linkage or suggestive linkage to chromosome 2, and noted that FAME2 is the most frequently observed linked locus in Caucasian patients.
